paper.title: RFC 8949: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), Appendix A (Examples of Encoded CBOR Data Items)

program.how: written for ounce-core from the RFC's description of the initial byte, argument sizes, preferred (shortest) float serialization and indefinite-length items; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: All 81 examples of Appendix A Table 6 are built by the program's own encoder from their diagnostic notation (integers up to 2^64 and bignums, negative integers, 13 finite floats in half, single and double width, infinities and NaN in all three widths, false/true/null/undefined and simple values, tags, byte and text strings including U+00FC, U+6C34 and U+10151, nested arrays and maps, indefinite-length strings, arrays and maps) and give exactly the published bytes (81 of 81)
Each of the 81 published encodings is walked by a well-formedness decoder that consumes exactly its bytes and no more (81 of 81)
The 22 float examples decode from their published bytes back to the value written in diagnostic notation (22 of 22; the decimal literals such as 1.1 are parsed by the compiler)

expected_values_source.what: the encoded column of RFC 8949 Appendix A Table 6; examples.inc is generated from the fetched RFC text by a script, and the diagnostic values were entered by hand as encoder calls in table order (a wrong entry makes the byte comparison fail, it cannot make it pass)
expected_values_source.note: the simple-value numbers (false=20, true=21, null=22, undefined=23) are from RFC 8949 Table 4 in the same fetched text

negative_control: built with -DNEG=1 (negative integers encoded as -n instead of -1-n) 5 of 81 examples fail (-1, -10, -100, -1000 and the map containing -2; -1 encodes as 0x21 instead of 0x20) and the program exits 1; with -DNEG=2 (floats never shortened) 12 of 81 fail
not_checked: the full decoding rules: this program only checks well-formedness and the float values, not a complete decoder to diagnostic notation, duplicate map keys, UTF-8 validity or tag semantics
deterministic encoding (section 4.2) beyond the preferred float and integer forms: map key sorting is not tested
the appendix examples of other RFCs (CDDL, COSE) and CBOR sequences
speed (emulator run time says nothing about real hardware)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, reproduces the byte strings that RFC 8949 Appendix A publishes for its 81 examples. It does not show that the encoder is a complete CBOR implementation.
